```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
```

This article shows how {gratia} works with models fitted using `mgcv::gfam()`.
This family lets groups of observations follow different distributions in
the same model.
It covers plotting shared and family-specific smooths, predicting and
simulating responses for each family, and checking the fitted model. A
simulated example with binary and count observations illustrates these
operations.

## An example with binary and count responses

Suppose one bird survey records whether a species was detected, while another
counts how many birds of that species were seen. Both surveys can help describe
how records vary with woodland cover. We fit them together using `mgcv::gfam()`
and assign a binomial or Poisson family to each observation. gratia uses those
assignments for predictions, simulations and checks of the fitted model.

The two surveys provide separate observations. For a single response with
zeros and positive values, a delta model estimates the probability of a
positive response and the distribution of the positive values. See the
[worked delta-model example](sdmTMB-support.html).

We simulate fixed-effort surveys at independent sites. The log odds of
detection and the log expected count have different intercepts but share the
same smooth response to woodland cover. Sharing the curve assumes that a
change in cover has the same effect on log odds and log expected count. We
compare this assumption with survey-specific curves below.

The example uses {mgcv} for fitting, {dplyr} to summarise results and {ggplot2}
for plots.

```{r packages}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
library("dplyr")
library("ggplot2")
```

We generate 300 detection records and 300 count records, then plot the
observations against woodland cover for each survey. The shared `habitat()`
function supplies the curved effect on both linear predictors.

```{r surveys}
set.seed(241)
survey <- data.frame(
  woodland = runif(600),
  source = factor(rep(c("Detection", "Count"), each = 300),
    levels = c("Detection", "Count"))
)
survey$family_id <- as.integer(survey$source)
habitat <- function(x) 1.8 * sin(pi * x) - 0.8 * x
eta <- ifelse(survey$source == "Detection", -1.3, 0.2) +
  habitat(survey$woodland)
survey$observed <- ifelse(survey$source == "Detection",
  rbinom(600, size = 1, prob = plogis(eta)),
  rpois(600, lambda = exp(eta)))
ggplot(survey, aes(woodland, observed)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~ source, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Proportion of woodland", y = "Survey response")
```

The binary panel contains only zero and one. The count panel has a wider range
and variance that grows with the mean. A binomial family with one trial and a
Poisson family are appropriate for the simulated surveys. For real counts,
extra variation may require `nb()` instead of Poisson; residual checks help
assess that choice.

## Fit a shared smooth with different response families

The first response column holds the observation and the second gives its
family's position in the list. Family 1 is binomial and family 2 is Poisson.
The factor `source` gives each survey its own intercept, and `s(woodland)`
gives both linear predictors the same smooth. REML estimates its smoothness.

```{r fit}
joint <- gam(cbind(observed, family_id) ~ source + s(woodland, k = 10),
  data = survey, family = gfam(list(binomial(), poisson())), method = "REML")
draw(joint, parametric = FALSE)
```

A change of $d$ in the smooth multiplies both detection odds and expected
count by $\exp(d)$. The fitted smooth rises towards intermediate cover and
then declines, as in the simulation. To recover the fitted detection probability
or expected count, add the survey's intercept to the smooth and apply that
family's inverse link.

The [mgcv grouped-family documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/gfam.html)
explains the response encoding and how to share terms.

Sharing a smooth can improve precision if its assumption is reasonable. A model
with different smooths provides a useful comparison when the surveys have enough
information to estimate them:

```{r different-responses}
separate <- gam(cbind(observed, family_id) ~ source +
    s(woodland, by = source, k = 10),
  data = survey, family = gfam(list(binomial(), poisson())), method = "REML")
draw(separate, parametric = FALSE)
```

Both fitted curves peak at intermediate woodland cover. The wider intervals
for the binary survey show that its curve is estimated less precisely. If
survey effort varies and the expected count is proportional to effort, use a
log-effort offset for the Poisson observations. Model the effect of effort on
detection probability separately.

## Predict the appropriate quantity for each survey

Prediction rows must identify their distribution. This matters even if their
covariates are identical. We generate the same cover grid for both surveys
and pass `family_index` explicitly. Response-scale `fitted_samples()` applies
each row's inverse link to every shared coefficient draw.

```{r predictions}
grid <- expand.grid(woodland = seq(0, 1, length.out = 80),
  source = levels(survey$source))
grid$source <- factor(grid$source, levels = levels(survey$source))
index <- as.integer(grid$source)
means <- fitted_samples(joint, data = grid, family_index = index,
  n_draws = 200, seed = 242)
intervals <- means |>
  group_by(.row) |>
  summarise(estimate = median(.fitted), lower = quantile(.fitted, 0.025),
    upper = quantile(.fitted, 0.975), .groups = "drop")
curves <- bind_cols(grid, intervals |> select(-.row))
ggplot(curves, aes(woodland, estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ source, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Proportion of woodland", y = "Expected survey response")
```

The curves show detection probabilities and expected counts, with pointwise
intervals. Each coefficient draw is used for both surveys, so the intervals
come from predictions that share the same woodland effect in each draw.

To compare these means with mgcv's own predictions, supply both columns of the
response expression in the prediction data. `family_id` selects the response
family; the placeholder `observed` value is ignored during prediction:

```{r native-means}
native_grid <- transform(grid, observed = 0, family_id = index)
head(data.frame(grid, expected = predict(joint, native_grid, type = "response")))
```

Use `simulate()` to draw future observations at these cover values, holding the
fitted coefficients and any other distribution parameters fixed. These draws
show variation in individual observations. Use `posterior_samples()` to
include coefficient uncertainty in the draws as well.

```{r response-draws}
replicates <- simulate(joint, data = grid, family_index = index,
  nsim = 200, seed = 243)
future <- data.frame(grid, lower = apply(replicates, 1, quantile, 0.025),
  upper = apply(replicates, 1, quantile, 0.975))
future |>
  filter(woodland > 0.49, woodland < 0.51)
```

Even a precisely estimated detection probability yields individual responses
of zero or one. Individual counts also vary around their fitted mean. The
`family_index` values must match the positions of the response families in
the fitted model.

## Check the fit separately for each response family

Raw residual magnitudes are not comparable between binary and count responses.
Probability integral transform (PIT) residuals locate each observation in its
own fitted distribution. At a discrete observation, gratia randomises within
its probability mass; quantile residuals transform those probabilities to
standard-normal scores. See [Model diagnostics](model-checking.html) for the
reference calculations and the distinction from posterior predictive checks.
Setting `by_family = TRUE` gives separate panels for the binary and count
responses:

```{r checks, fig.height=6}
appraise(joint, type = "quantile", by_family = TRUE, seed = 244)
```

Separate panels help you see whether a pattern is confined to one survey.
Look for departures in the tails of the QQ plots, changes in residual spread
across the fitted values, or disagreement between the observed and fitted
responses. Here the quantile residuals for both families broadly agree with
their references.

Pooling standard-normal residuals is also possible. The colours retain each
component's identity; histogram densities are calculated separately with
common bin edges. Traditional deviance or response residuals instead default
to separate component facets because their scales differ. We draw the pooled
histogram, then use a worm plot with separate family panels. A worm plot
subtracts the reference quantile, so a well-fitting model should give points
scattered around zero:

```{r pooled-check}
residuals_hist_plot(joint, type = "quantile", by_family = FALSE, seed = 244)
worm_plot(joint, type = "quantile", by_family = TRUE, seed = 244)
```

The worm plot's separate panels show which response family contributes each
pattern.

Next, compare the observed binary and count distributions with replicated
datasets. `posterior_predictive_plot()` includes uncertainty in the fitted
coefficients when generating these replicates:

```{r predictive-check}
posterior_predictive_plot(joint, n = 50, seed = 245)
```

The count panel has some departures at individual counts, despite reasonable
overall shape agreement. Its intervals are pointwise and have appreciable
simulation error with 50 replicates; increase that number before judging
individual probability masses closely.

The bars show how the proportion at each response value varies between
replicated surveys. This checks the detection frequency in the binary survey
and the distribution of counts in the other survey.

## Using other families, weights and prediction data

`gfam()` accepts ordinary and extended mgcv families with a scalar response,
including negative binomial, Tweedie, beta, scaled-t and ordered categories.
gratia can simulate ordered-category responses. For an ordinal component,
request `fitted_samples(..., quantity = "expectation")` to obtain category
probabilities, with categories identified by `.category`. Link-scale fitted
draws are also available. General families with several linear predictors
are not `gfam()` components.

Missing required predictors or membership give missing predictions. Missing
responses alone do not prevent prediction. With `na.exclude()`, excluded fitting
rows are restored as `NA` in fitted draws and simulations, while checks use the
observations actually fitted.

For scalar censored components, `simulate()` generates uncensored responses.
For a custom comparison with censored observations, apply the same censoring
rule to each simulated dataset before comparing the distributions.
`posterior_predictive_plot()` is unavailable for censored components. Matrix
responses that encode censoring or binomial success and failure counts are
outside the scope of `gfam()`.

For grouped binomial proportions, supply the number of trials in `weights`;
for Gaussian and Gamma components these weights represent response precision.
Prediction data default to weights of one unless you supply them. These
interpretations differ and should follow how the observations were collected.

Use the component diagnostics to assess the observation distributions and the
separate-curve comparison to decide whether to share the cover response.
